# Mission

Produce an evidence-backed decision package for Yiming ΓÇ£TimΓÇ¥ Zhao, a Stanford
EE PhD student in the Senesky group, covering only the following requested
questions:

1. Review at least 150 high-quality, credible, peer-reviewed papers spanning
   the advisor groupΓÇÖs GaN/SiC/wide-bandgap device fields and relevant fusion,
   plasma, stellarator, magnetic-diagnostic, and instrumentation fields.
2. Decide whether the original directionΓÇöGaN Hall-effect magnetic diagnostics
   for in-situ magnetic-confinement-fusion measurementsΓÇöis publishable and
   strategically strong; if not, determine whether to adjust it or change
   direction.
3. Prefer paths that minimize new cleanroom work, reuse established device
   topologies, and place defensible novelty in application, calibration,
   measurement architecture, simulation, data analysis, inverse methods, or
   software.
4. Review the submitted IEEE Sensors Letters manuscript, its source files,
   available HSX data, and the 23-Jul-2026 decision/reviewer comments.
5. Compare a revised Sensors Letters submission against the userΓÇÖs proposed
   route of an arXiv preprint plus a substantially completed Review of
   Scientific Instruments study using the next HSX campaign.
6. Specify the next experiment and analysis needed to close calibration,
   absolute-field, repeatability, uncertainty, bandwidth, conventional-probe
   comparison, and novelty gaps.
7. Screen only the concepts already supported by the supplied work for
   potentially protectable subject matter before public disclosure. This is a
   research screen, not a legal opinion or a patentability conclusion.
8. Produce a realistic 24-month PhD plan aligned with the goal of graduating
   in about two years and preparing for a startup afterward.

## Fixed preferences and constraints

- Use the supplied files as ground truth; state conflicts explicitly.
- Do not fabricate, infer, or ΓÇ£correctΓÇ¥ measured values.
- No new neutron or gamma experiments are in scope.
- Do not broaden the mission into unrelated startup ideas or unrelated PhD
  fields.
- Keep laboratory and cleanroom burden low unless an experiment is essential
  to a publication gate.
- Separate facts, calculations, interpretations, proposals, unknowns, and
  legal questions.
- Make no external submission, disclosure, email, purchase, filing, account
  change, or cloud-document mutation.
- Treat international-student status as a scheduling and career constraint,
  not as a basis for immigration or legal advice.

## Completion condition

The mission is complete only when all stages in `EXECUTION_PLAN.md` pass their
acceptance checks, the 150-paper ledger passes deterministic validation, the
independent red-team corrections are incorporated, and
`outputs/FINAL_AUDIT.md` states `FINAL STATUS: PASS`.

# Source policy

## The 150-paper minimum

`outputs/01_SOURCE_LEDGER.csv` must contain at least 150 unique sources whose
`peer_review_status` is exactly `verified_peer_reviewed`.

Count only:

- journal articles with a verified journal/publisher record;
- peer-reviewed conference papers when the proceedings and review status are
  verified;
- peer-reviewed review articles.

Do not count:

- arXiv or other preprints;
- patents;
- theses or dissertations;
- vendor/application notes;
- standards;
- books or book chapters unless peer review is independently established;
- news, blogs, university pages, grant pages, or AI summaries;
- a paper whose publication status cannot be verified.

Those sources may appear in separate contextual or prior-art ledgers, but not
in the 150-paper count.

## Required ledger schema

The exact CSV header is:

```text
source_id,citation,title,authors,year,venue,doi,url,source_type,peer_review_status,quality_tier,topic_tags,claims_supported,verification_basis,access_level,notes
```

Rules:

- `source_id` is stable and unique (`S0001`, `S0002`, ...).
- Prefer DOI URLs (`https://doi.org/...`); otherwise use an official publisher
  record.
- `quality_tier` is `A`, `B`, or `C`, with a written rubric in
  `outputs/01_SOURCE_COVERAGE.md`.
- `access_level` is `full_text`, `abstract_metadata`, or `metadata_only`.
- Do not imply full-text review for an abstract-only or metadata-only source.
- `topic_tags` is semicolon-separated and must support coverage auditing.
- Deduplicate by normalized DOI first, then normalized title.

## Quality and breadth

Prioritize established journals, strong field venues, seminal papers, recent
high-quality work, and primary research. The combined ledger must materially
cover:

- AlGaN/GaN and other WBG Hall/device physics;
- Hall-sensor geometry, sensitivity, offset, noise, bandwidth, temperature,
  radiation context, packaging, and calibration;
- magnetic-confinement fusion and plasma magnetic diagnostics;
- stellarator/HSX-relevant field measurement and validation;
- direct sensors versus inductive/B-dot/Mirnov diagnostics and drift;
- uncertainty, repeatability, calibration traceability, and instrumentation;
- low-fabrication novelty through modeling, inverse methods, data fusion,
  signal processing, software, ML/control, or digital-twin methods.

Search until the verified, deduplicated minimum is met. A search result snippet
alone is not verification.

## Citation use

Every material claim in final reports must cite one or more `source_id` values
and include a stable link. Cite the supplied manuscript/data by filename and
page/figure/section rather than assigning them peer-reviewed source IDs.

# Checkpoint protocol

The package uses independent durable layers so a manually closed PowerShell
window does not erase the recovery state.

| Layer | Path | Update frequency |
|---|---|---|
| Raw Claude events | `logs/run_*/<stage>/*/stream.jsonl` | every emitted event, flushed immediately |
| Compact event index | `state/CLAUDE_EVENT_LOG.jsonl` | every emitted event, flushed immediately |
| Lifecycle operations | `state/OPERATION_LOG.csv` | preflight, attempt, downgrade, quarantine, validation, completion, handoff |
| Model/effort ledger | `state/MODEL_EFFORT_LOG.csv` | after every attempt/probe |
| Session index | `state/SESSION_INDEX.csv` | after every attempt |
| Attempt state | `state/attempts/<stage>.json` | before and after each attempt/transition |
| Completion marker | `state/markers/<stage>.done.json` | only after validation |
| Handoff snapshot | `state/CHATGPT_HANDOFF_STATE.json` and `.md` | attempt start, every stream change, and every transition |
| Effective prompts | `state/generated_prompts/<stage>_attempt_<n>.md` | before every attempt |

Claude also updates `state/PROJECT_STATE.md`, `state/WORKLOG.md`, partial
outputs, and `state/checkpoints/CP_<stage>_<timestamp>.md` during substantive
work.

## Manual interruption

If the user closes PowerShell after a long period without output, the last
flushed stream event and handoff JSON remain authoritative. The ChatGPT Windows
continuation must treat `CLAUDE_IN_PROGRESS` as an interrupted attempt, inspect
partial files, and resume without repeating valid work.

## Rejected-model outputs

Files produced by a downgraded or unverifiable-model attempt are moved under
the corresponding `logs/run_*/<stage>/rejected_attempt_*_outputs` directory
with `QUARANTINE_MANIFEST.json`. They remain available for audit but are not
accepted as stage outputs.

I would like a detailed timeline and strategies that can helpful to my PhD career after your early analysis.

Second, I would like you to review my publication, data, and the reviewer feedback. 448	\section{Introduction}
449	\IEEEPARstart{M}{agnetic} confinement fusion offers the prospect of clean, carbon-free baseload energy, and is regarded as a critical long-term option for future energy supply~\cite{Ongena2016}. Modern fusion experiments increasingly rely on data-driven modeling and machine-learning--based control, placing growing demands on in-situ plasma diagnostics and the associated instrumentation~\cite{Degrave2022, Anirudh2023}. Magnetic field diagnostics are essential for monitoring plasma position, shape, stability, and stored energy in magnetic confinement fusion devices such as tokamaks and stellarators~\cite{ref1}. As fusion experiments advance toward long-pulse and steady-state operation~\cite{ref2}, in-situ diagnostics must provide reliable, real-time measurements of plasma-generated magnetic fields for equilibrium reconstruction and control. Conventional diagnostic systems with inductive sensors, such as Mirnov coils, recover the magnetic field by integrating the induced voltage proportional to its time derivative. During extended operation, this integration becomes problematic as it accumulates low-frequency noise and radiation-induced offsets, leading to drift and reduced accuracy in tracking magnetic fields~\cite{ref3}, \cite{ref4}.
450	
451	Hall-effect sensors offer an attractive alternative because they enable direct magnetic field measurement without integration, eliminating drift at the source~\cite{ref5}, \cite{ref6}. However, conventional Hall-effect devices based on silicon, gallium arsenide (GaAs), indium arsenide (InAs), and indium antimonide (InSb) platforms cannot be deployed near the plasma edge because the in-vessel environment combines elevated temperature, vacuum operation, chemical reactivity, and radiation exposure. Gallium nitride (GaN) is a wide-bandgap semiconductor with strong thermal tolerance, making it well suited for harsh-environment electronics and in-situ sensing~\cite{ref7}, \cite{ref8}. In AlGaN/GaN heterostructures, a two-dimensional electron gas (2DEG) forms at the interface~\cite{ref9}. Consequently, the high electron mobility of this 2DEG channel enables high sensitivity ideal for this application~\cite{ref10}. In prior thermal characterization experiments, AlGaN/GaN Hall-effect sensors maintained stable current-scaled sensitivity from room temperature up to \SI{576}{\degreeCelsius}~\cite{ref11}, supporting their potential for extreme-environment magnetic field sensing~\cite{ref12}.
452	
453	\IEEEpubidadjcol In this work, we demonstrate an AlGaN/GaN Hall-effect sensor for in-situ magnetic field monitoring inside the Helically Symmetric eXperiment (HSX), the first stellarator designed and built with a quasi-helically symmetric magnetic field, operated at a \SI{1}{\tesla} on-axis magnetic field~\cite{ref13}, \cite{ref14}. The Hall-effect sensor was fabricated, packaged for ultra-high-vacuum and high-temperature operation, and deployed near the plasma edge. By comparing biased and unbiased operation, plasma-discharge and coil-only shots, and the sensor output with conventional plasma stored-energy diagnostics, we validate that the packaged AlGaN/GaN Hall-effect sensor can detect plasma-dependent magnetic field dynamics in real time, with a 1 MHz readout bandwidth across 68 consecutive shots.

455	\section{Sensor Fabrication and Experimental Setup}
456	\subsection{Fabrication}
457	The AlGaN/GaN wafer, purchased from NTT Advanced Technology Corporation, consists of a \SI{3.7}{\micro\meter} buffer structure, a \SI{300}{\nano\meter} GaN layer, a \SI{1}{\nano\meter} AlN spacer, and a \SI{22}{\nano\meter} Al$_{0.28}$Ga$_{0.72}$N barrier layer. The Hall-effect sensors were fabricated at the Stanford Nanofabrication Facility. The fabrication process began with a mesa etch of the III-nitride layer to define the active regions, followed by deposition and rapid thermal annealing of a Ti~(\SI{25}{\nano\meter})/Al~(\SI{200}{\nano\meter})/Mo~(\SI{40}{\nano\meter})/Au~(\SI{80}{\nano\meter}) stack at \SI{850}{\degreeCelsius} for \SI{35}{\second} to form Ohmic contacts~\cite{ref11}. A \SI{7}{\nano\meter}-thick Al$_2$O$_3$ passivation layer was then deposited; vias were etched to expose the contacts; and a Ti/Au bond-metal layer was deposited for wire bonding. The wafer was singulated into \SI{5}{\milli\meter} $\times$ \SI{5}{\milli\meter} dies for packaging. Fig.~\ref{fig:fab}(a) shows a cross-sectional schematic of the AlGaN/GaN Hall-effect sensor. The fabricated Hall-effect sensors feature a regular octagonal geometry with an inscribed diameter of \SI{200}{\micro\meter}~\cite{ref10}, as illustrated in Fig.~\ref{fig:fab}(b).

464	\subsection{Packaging}
465	The individual die was wire-bonded to a ceramic leadless chip carrier (LCC; Spectrum Semiconductor Materials) using aluminum wire. The die and wire bonds were then encapsulated with epoxy (EPO-TEK 353ND) and vacuum-baked at \SI{150}{\degreeCelsius} for 1~hour to meet the ultra-high-vacuum (UHV) requirements of the HSX facility. The packaged sensor was mounted on a custom zirconia ceramic holder attached to a stainless-steel standoff for insertion into the HSX vessel. To reduce the risk of arcing and epoxy degradation during glow discharge cleaning (GDC) and plasma operations, a grounded graphite shield was installed over the packaged sensor module. The packaged sensor assembly and its in-vessel placement are shown in Fig.~\ref{fig:pkg}.

478	\subsection{Experimental Setup}
479	The Hall-effect sensor module was deployed inside the HSX vessel near the plasma edge, as shown in Fig.~\ref{fig:pkg}. The bias supply, readout electronics, and data acquisition system were located outside the vessel and connected to the sensor through vacuum feedthroughs. During operation, the sensor was voltage-biased and generated a transverse Hall-effect voltage given by
480	\begin{equation}
481	V_{H} = S_{v} V_{\mathrm{bias}} B,
482	\end{equation}
483	where $S_{v}$ is the voltage-scaled sensitivity, $B$ is the orthogonal magnetic field, and $V_{\mathrm{bias}}$ is the bias voltage. As illustrated in Fig.~\ref{fig:readout}, two opposite terminals of the Hall-effect plate were biased using the built-in waveform generator of an oscilloscope (Keysight DSOX1204G), while the Hall-effect voltage was measured across the orthogonal terminals. The differential Hall-effect voltage was amplified by a readout circuit consisting of an instrumentation amplifier (Texas Instruments INA849) followed by two operational amplifier (Texas Instruments OPA814) stages, providing a total voltage gain of \SI[per-mode=symbol]{200}{\volt\per\volt} and a bandwidth of \SI{1}{\mega\hertz}. The amplified output voltage can be expressed as
484	\begin{equation}
485	V_{\mathrm{out}} = A_{v} V_{H} + V_{\mathrm{off}},
486	\end{equation}
487	where $A_{v}$ is the voltage gain and $V_{\mathrm{off}}$ accounts for offset contributions from the sensor and amplifier stages. The amplified output was continuously monitored during the plasma discharge shots. In this readout chain, $V_{\mathrm{off}}$ is bias-independent but may vary with temperature during operation~\cite{ref15}. Since $V_{H}$ scales linearly with $V_{\mathrm{bias}}$ whereas $V_{\mathrm{off}}$ does not, comparing the sensor output under biased ($V_{\mathrm{bias}} = \SI{0.4}{\volt}$) and unbiased ($V_{\mathrm{bias}} = \SI{0}{\volt}$) operation isolates the bias-dependent Hall-effect response from the offset and from other artifacts such as electromagnetic pickup or charge-induced response. Absolute calibration of $V_{\mathrm{off}}$ and quantitative correction for its temperature dependence remain future work.

494	\section{Results and Discussion}
495	\subsection{Sensor Functionality}
496	The packaged AlGaN/GaN Hall-effect sensor was deployed inside the HSX stellarator and operated across 68 consecutive shots. Prior to each plasma discharge, mechanical energy stored in 18 motor generators was converted to electrical current driving the 48 magnetic field coils of HSX; after approximately \SI{800}{\milli\second} the coils' current saturated, establishing the target magnetic confinement field. Plasma was then ignited within the resulting \SI{50}{\milli\second} flat-top period using up to \SI{200}{\kilo\watt} of \SI{28}{\giga\hertz} electron cyclotron resonance heating (ECRH). Fig.~\ref{fig:func}(a) compares the amplified output of the Hall-effect sensor when unbiased ($V_{\mathrm{bias}} = \SI{0}{\volt}$; shot 63) and when biased at $V_{\mathrm{bias}} = \SI{0.4}{\volt}$ (shot 65). Consistent with the Hall-effect voltage dependence on $V_{\mathrm{bias}}$, the unbiased output remains near a low baseline, whereas the biased output increases during coil ramp-up and shows a sharp transient followed by fluctuations during the plasma discharge. To separate the plasma-induced response from the background coil field, Fig.~\ref{fig:func}(b) compares a plasma discharge (shot 65) with a coil-only shot (shot 68). Both traces show a similar increase during coil ramp-up, but only the plasma discharge exhibits the pronounced transient and subsequent fluctuations near plasma ignition. These results confirm that the packaged sensor remained functional in the HSX environment and detected magnetic field variations associated with plasma dynamics, with the ignition transient consistent with the diamagnetic response of the confined plasma as plasma pressure rises and expels magnetic flux. Across the 68 discharge shots, the shape and timing of this transient repeated reliably under comparable conditions, indicating stable sensor operation throughout the deployment.

503	\subsection{Real-Time Plasma Energy Tracking}
504	The measurements shown in Fig.~\ref{fig:track} compare the amplified output of the in-vessel AlGaN/GaN Hall-effect sensor with the plasma stored energy measured by the HSX diamagnetic loop diagnostic~\cite{ref16} for three representative discharge conditions. The two diagnostic methods measure physically distinct quantities: the Hall-effect sensor probes the local magnetic field at a single in-vessel location, whereas the diamagnetic loop measures the change in enclosed toroidal flux from which volumetric plasma stored energy is inferred. Both, however, respond to plasma magnetic dynamics and are therefore expected to be temporally correlated~\cite{ref1}. The two signals are acquired through separate data acquisition systems with a known $\sim$\SI{30}{\milli\second} relative timing offset arising from delayed triggering of the diamagnetic loop DAQ. In the high-energy discharge (shot 21) shown in Fig.~\ref{fig:track}(a) and (a$'$), the rapid rise and sustained stored-energy plateau are accompanied by a pronounced sensor response and elevated fluctuations during the discharge. In the late-breakdown case (shot 18) shown in Fig.~\ref{fig:track}(b) and (b$'$), the sensor output remains near baseline until the delayed rise in plasma stored energy, after which a clear increase in signal amplitude is observed. In contrast, for the failed-breakdown case (shot 19) shown in Fig.~\ref{fig:track}(c) and (c$'$), both the stored energy and the sensor output remain near baseline. Although quantitative calibration remains future work, the consistent temporal agreement across these discharge scenarios establishes that the AlGaN/GaN Hall-effect sensor can track plasma-dependent magnetic-field dynamics in real time.
505	\section{Conclusion}
506	An AlGaN/GaN Hall-effect sensor was fabricated, packaged, and deployed inside the HSX stellarator (\SI{1}{\tesla} on-axis field, up to \SI{200}{\kilo\watt} of ECRH) for in-situ magnetic-field monitoring near the plasma edge. The packaged device operated through 68 consecutive shots under ultra-high-vacuum and elevated-temperature conditions. Comparisons between biased and unbiased operation, together with plasma-discharge and coil-only measurements, confirmed that the observed response was associated with magnetic field changes detected through the biased Hall-effect sensor. The amplified sensor output further showed temporal agreement with conventional plasma stored-energy diagnostics across high-energy, late-breakdown, and failed-breakdown scenarios. Although quantitative calibration remains future work, these results establish AlGaN/GaN Hall-effect sensors as a feasible platform for real-time magnetic diagnostics in fusion-relevant environments. Future work will focus on absolute calibration through in-situ cross-reference with established HSX magnetic diagnostics~\cite{ref17}, extended-duration deployments in HSX to evaluate offset stability, radiation and neutron irradiation characterization at a dedicated facility to assess radiation hardness, and integration of lower-noise readout electronics for resolving smaller-amplitude magnetohydrodynamic fluctuations.

\begin{abstract}[graphical_abstract]
Direct magnetic field sensors can address integration drift commonly observed in conventional inductive magnetic diagnostics used in fusion systems. In this work, an AlGaN/GaN Hall-effect sensor was fabricated, packaged, and deployed inside the Helically Symmetric eXperiment (HSX)---the first quasi-helically symmetric stellarator, operating with a 1 T on-axis magnetic field and up to 200 kW of launched electron cyclotron resonance heating (ECRH) power---for in-situ magnetic field monitoring near the plasma edge. The sensor leverages the high-mobility two-dimensional electron gas (2DEG) formed in the AlGaN/GaN heterostructure for sensitive magnetic field measurement, while the wide-bandgap GaN material system provides thermal robustness for harsh-environment operation. During 68 consecutive plasma discharge shots, the sensor remained functional and produced clear transient responses associated with plasma ignition and discharge dynamics. Comparisons between biased and unbiased operation, as well as plasma-discharge and coil-only shots, confirmed that the response originated from the biased Hall-effect sensor element. \section{Introduction}
\IEEEPARstart{M}{agnetic} confinement fusion offers the prospect of clean, carbon-free baseload energy, and is regarded as a critical long-term option for future energy supply~\cite{Ongena2016}. Modern fusion experiments increasingly rely on data-driven modeling and machine-learning--based control, placing growing demands on in-situ plasma diagnostics and the associated instrumentation~\cite{Degrave2022, Anirudh2023}. Magnetic field diagnostics are essential for monitoring plasma position, shape, stability, and stored energy in magnetic confinement fusion devices such as tokamaks and stellarators~\cite{ref1}. As fusion experiments advance toward long-pulse and steady-state operation~\cite{ref2}, in-situ diagnostics must provide reliable, real-time measurements of plasma-generated magnetic fields for equilibrium reconstruction and control. Conventional diagnostic systems with inductive sensors, such as Mirnov coils, recover the magnetic field by integrating the induced voltage proportional to its time derivative. During extended operation, this integration becomes problematic as it accumulates low-frequency noise and radiation-induced offsets, leading to drift and reduced accuracy in tracking magnetic fields~\cite{ref3}, \cite{ref4}.

Hall-effect sensors offer an attractive alternative because they enable direct magnetic field measurement without integration, eliminating drift at the source~\cite{ref5}, \cite{ref6}. However, conventional Hall-effect devices based on silicon, gallium arsenide (GaAs), indium arsenide (InAs), and indium antimonide (InSb) platforms cannot be deployed near the plasma edge because the in-vessel environment combines elevated temperature, vacuum operation, chemical reactivity, and radiation exposure. Gallium nitride (GaN) is a wide-bandgap semiconductor with strong thermal tolerance, making it well suited for harsh-environment electronics and in-situ sensing~\cite{ref7}, \cite{ref8}. In AlGaN/GaN heterostructures, a two-dimensional electron gas (2DEG) forms at the interface~\cite{ref9}. Consequently, the high electron mobility of this 2DEG channel enables high sensitivity ideal for this application~\cite{ref10}. In prior thermal characterization experiments, AlGaN/GaN Hall-effect sensors maintained stable current-scaled sensitivity from room temperature up to \SI{576}{\degreeCelsius}~\cite{ref11}, supporting their potential for extreme-environment magnetic field sensing~\cite{ref12}.

\IEEEpubidadjcol In this work, we demonstrate an AlGaN/GaN Hall-effect sensor for in-situ magnetic field monitoring inside the Helically Symmetric eXperiment (HSX), the first stellarator designed and built with a quasi-helically symmetric magnetic field, operated at a \SI{1}{\tesla} on-axis magnetic field~\cite{ref13}, \cite{ref14}. The Hall-effect sensor was fabricated, packaged for ultra-high-vacuum and high-temperature operation, and deployed near the plasma edge. By comparing biased and unbiased operation, plasma-discharge and coil-only shots, and the sensor output with conventional plasma stored-energy diagnostics, we validate that the packaged AlGaN/GaN Hall-effect sensor can detect plasma-dependent magnetic field dynamics in real time, with a 1 MHz readout bandwidth across 68 consecutive shots.
% \newpage
\section{Sensor Fabrication and Experimental Setup}
\subsection{Fabrication}
The AlGaN/GaN wafer, purchased from NTT Advanced Technology Corporation, consists of a \SI{3.7}{\micro\meter} buffer structure, a \SI{300}{\nano\meter} GaN layer, a \SI{1}{\nano\meter} AlN spacer, and a \SI{22}{\nano\meter} Al$_{0.28}$Ga$_{0.72}$N barrier layer. The Hall-effect sensors were fabricated at the Stanford Nanofabrication Facility. The fabrication process began with a mesa etch of the III-nitride layer to define the active regions, followed by deposition and rapid thermal annealing of a Ti~(\SI{25}{\nano\meter})/Al~(\SI{200}{\nano\meter})/Mo~(\SI{40}{\nano\meter})/Au~(\SI{80}{\nano\meter}) stack at \SI{850}{\degreeCelsius} for \SI{35}{\second} to form Ohmic contacts~\cite{ref11}. A \SI{7}{\nano\meter}-thick Al$_2$O$_3$ passivation layer was then deposited; vias were etched to expose the contacts; and a Ti/Au bond-metal layer was deposited for wire bonding. The wafer was singulated into \SI{5}{\milli\meter} $\times$ \SI{5}{\milli\meter} dies for packaging. Fig.~\ref{fig:fab}(a) shows a cross-sectional schematic of the AlGaN/GaN Hall-effect sensor. The fabricated Hall-effect sensors feature a regular octagonal geometry with an inscribed diameter of \SI{200}{\micro\meter}~\cite{ref10}, as illustrated in Fig.~\ref{fig:fab}(b).
\begin{figure}[!t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{./figures/fig1.pdf}
\caption{Fabricated AlGaN/GaN Hall-effect sensor. (a) Cross-sectional schematic of the passivated AlGaN/GaN Hall-effect sensor showing the 2DEG sensing layer, Ohmic contacts, Al$_2$O$_3$ passivation, and bond metal. (b) Optical image of the fabricated regular octagonal Hall-effect plate with a 200 \textmu m inscribed diameter.}
\label{fig:fab}
\end{figure}
\subsection{Packaging}
The individual die was wire-bonded to a ceramic leadless chip carrier (LCC; Spectrum Semiconductor Materials) using aluminum wire. The die and wire bonds were then encapsulated with epoxy (EPO-TEK 353ND) and vacuum-baked at \SI{150}{\degreeCelsius} for 1~hour to meet the ultra-high-vacuum (UHV) requirements of the HSX facility. The packaged sensor was mounted on a custom zirconia ceramic holder attached to a stainless-steel standoff for insertion into the HSX vessel. To reduce the risk of arcing and epoxy degradation during glow discharge cleaning (GDC) and plasma operations, a grounded graphite shield was installed over the packaged sensor module. The packaged sensor assembly and its in-vessel placement are shown in Fig.~\ref{fig:pkg}.
\begin{figure}[!t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{./figures/fig2.pdf}
\caption{Packaging and in-vessel deployment of the AlGaN/GaN Hall-effect sensor in HSX. The sensor die was wire-bonded to a ceramic leadless chip carrier, epoxy-coated, and mounted on a custom flange for insertion into the HSX vessel near the plasma edge.}
\label{fig:pkg}
\end{figure}
\begin{figure}
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{./figures/fig3.pdf}
\caption{Experimental readout configuration for the in-vessel Hall-effect sensor. The sensor was voltage-biased using the built-in waveform generator of an oscilloscope, and the transverse Hall voltage was amplified using a differential readout chain before data acquisition.}
\label{fig:readout}
\end{figure}
\subsection{Experimental Setup}
The Hall-effect sensor module was deployed inside the HSX vessel near the plasma edge, as shown in Fig.~\ref{fig:pkg}. The bias supply, readout electronics, and data acquisition system were located outside the vessel and connected to the sensor through vacuum feedthroughs. During operation, the sensor was voltage-biased and generated a transverse Hall-effect voltage given by
\begin{equation}
V_{H} = S_{v} V_{\mathrm{bias}} B,
\end{equation}
where $S_{v}$ is the voltage-scaled sensitivity, $B$ is the orthogonal magnetic field, and $V_{\mathrm{bias}}$ is the bias voltage. As illustrated in Fig.~\ref{fig:readout}, two opposite terminals of the Hall-effect plate were biased using the built-in waveform generator of an oscilloscope (Keysight DSOX1204G), while the Hall-effect voltage was measured across the orthogonal terminals. The differential Hall-effect voltage was amplified by a readout circuit consisting of an instrumentation amplifier (Texas Instruments INA849) followed by two operational amplifier (Texas Instruments OPA814) stages, providing a total voltage gain of \SI[per-mode=symbol]{200}{\volt\per\volt} and a bandwidth of \SI{1}{\mega\hertz}. The amplified output voltage can be expressed as
\begin{equation}
V_{\mathrm{out}} = A_{v} V_{H} + V_{\mathrm{off}},
\end{equation}
where $A_{v}$ is the voltage gain and $V_{\mathrm{off}}$ accounts for offset contributions from the sensor and amplifier stages. The amplified output was continuously monitored during the plasma discharge shots. In this readout chain, $V_{\mathrm{off}}$ is bias-independent but may vary with temperature during operation~\cite{ref15}. Since $V_{H}$ scales linearly with $V_{\mathrm{bias}}$ whereas $V_{\mathrm{off}}$ does not, comparing the sensor output under biased ($V_{\mathrm{bias}} = \SI{0.4}{\volt}$) and unbiased ($V_{\mathrm{bias}} = \SI{0}{\volt}$) operation isolates the bias-dependent Hall-effect response from the offset and from other artifacts such as electromagnetic pickup or charge-induced response. Absolute calibration of $V_{\mathrm{off}}$ and quantitative correction for its temperature dependence remain future work.
\begin{figure}[!t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{./figures/fig4.eps}
\caption{Functional verification of the packaged AlGaN/GaN Hall-effect sensor during HSX operation. (a) Amplified sensor output for unbiased (shot 63) and biased (shot 65) operation. (b) Comparison of the biased sensor response during a plasma discharge (shot 65) and a coil-only shot (shot 68).}
\label{fig:func}
\end{figure}
\section{Results and Discussion}
\subsection{Sensor Functionality}
The packaged AlGaN/GaN Hall-effect sensor was deployed inside the HSX stellarator and operated across 68 consecutive shots. Prior to each plasma discharge, mechanical energy stored in 18 motor generators was converted to electrical current driving the 48 magnetic field coils of HSX; after approximately \SI{800}{\milli\second} the coils' current saturated, establishing the target magnetic confinement field. Plasma was then ignited within the resulting \SI{50}{\milli\second} flat-top period using up to \SI{200}{\kilo\watt} of \SI{28}{\giga\hertz} electron cyclotron resonance heating (ECRH). Fig.~\ref{fig:func}(a) compares the amplified output of the Hall-effect sensor when unbiased ($V_{\mathrm{bias}} = \SI{0}{\volt}$; shot 63) and when biased at $V_{\mathrm{bias}} = \SI{0.4}{\volt}$ (shot 65). Consistent with the Hall-effect voltage dependence on $V_{\mathrm{bias}}$, the unbiased output remains near a low baseline, whereas the biased output increases during coil ramp-up and shows a sharp transient followed by fluctuations during the plasma discharge. To separate the plasma-induced response from the background coil field, Fig.~\ref{fig:func}(b) compares a plasma discharge (shot 65) with a coil-only shot (shot 68). Both traces show a similar increase during coil ramp-up, but only the plasma discharge exhibits the pronounced transient and subsequent fluctuations near plasma ignition. These results confirm that the packaged sensor remained functional in the HSX environment and detected magnetic field variations associated with plasma dynamics, with the ignition transient consistent with the diamagnetic response of the confined plasma as plasma pressure rises and expels magnetic flux. Across the 68 discharge shots, the shape and timing of this transient repeated reliably under comparable conditions, indicating stable sensor operation throughout the deployment.
\begin{figure}[!t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{./figures/fig5.eps}
\caption{Real-time tracking of plasma-dependent magnetic-field dynamics. Plasma stored energy from conventional HSX diagnostics is compared with the amplified AlGaN/GaN Hall-effect sensor output for (a), (a$'$)~a high-energy discharge (shot 21); (b), (b$'$)~a late-breakdown discharge (shot 18); and (c), (c$'$)~a failed-breakdown case (shot 19). The two data acquisition systems have a $\sim$30 ms relative timing offset due to delayed triggering.}
\label{fig:track}
\end{figure}
\subsection{Real-Time Plasma Energy Tracking}
The measurements shown in Fig.~\ref{fig:track} compare the amplified output of the in-vessel AlGaN/GaN Hall-effect sensor with the plasma stored energy measured by the HSX diamagnetic loop diagnostic~\cite{ref16} for three representative discharge conditions. The two diagnostic methods measure physically distinct quantities: the Hall-effect sensor probes the local magnetic field at a single in-vessel location, whereas the diamagnetic loop measures the change in enclosed toroidal flux from which volumetric plasma stored energy is inferred. Both, however, respond to plasma magnetic dynamics and are therefore expected to be temporally correlated~\cite{ref1}. The two signals are acquired through separate data acquisition systems with a known $\sim$\SI{30}{\milli\second} relative timing offset arising from delayed triggering of the diamagnetic loop DAQ. In the high-energy discharge (shot 21) shown in Fig.~\ref{fig:track}(a) and (a$'$), the rapid rise and sustained stored-energy plateau are accompanied by a pronounced sensor response and elevated fluctuations during the discharge. In the late-breakdown case (shot 18) shown in Fig.~\ref{fig:track}(b) and (b$'$), the sensor output remains near baseline until the delayed rise in plasma stored energy, after which a clear increase in signal amplitude is observed. In contrast, for the failed-breakdown case (shot 19) shown in Fig.~\ref{fig:track}(c) and (c$'$), both the stored energy and the sensor output remain near baseline. Although quantitative calibration remains future work, the consistent temporal agreement across these discharge scenarios establishes that the AlGaN/GaN Hall-effect sensor can track plasma-dependent magnetic-field dynamics in real time.
\section{Conclusion}
An AlGaN/GaN Hall-effect sensor was fabricated, packaged, and deployed inside the HSX stellarator (\SI{1}{\tesla} on-axis field, up to \SI{200}{\kilo\watt} of ECRH) for in-situ magnetic-field monitoring near the plasma edge. The packaged device operated through 68 consecutive shots under ultra-high-vacuum and elevated-temperature conditions. Comparisons between biased and unbiased operation, together with plasma-discharge and coil-only measurements, confirmed that the observed response was associated with magnetic field changes detected through the biased Hall-effect sensor. The amplified sensor output further showed temporal agreement with conventional plasma stored-energy diagnostics across high-energy, late-breakdown, and failed-breakdown scenarios. Although quantitative calibration remains future work, these results establish AlGaN/GaN Hall-effect sensors as a feasible platform for real-time magnetic diagnostics in fusion-relevant environments. Future work will focus on absolute calibration through in-situ cross-reference with established HSX magnetic diagnostics~\cite{ref17}, extended-duration deployments in HSX to evaluate offset stability, radiation and neutron irradiation characterization at a dedicated facility to assess radiation hardness, and integration of lower-noise readout electronics for resolving smaller-amplitude magnetohydrodynamic fluctuations.

33	## Spinning phase table
34	
35	`state = (a2<<2) | (a1<<1) | a0`, advancing 0ΓåÆ7 each phase. Demod sign:
36	**+1 if a0 == a2 else ΓêÆ1** (a1 is irrelevant to the sign). Raw per-cycle
37	sign pattern: `+ ΓêÆ ΓêÆ + ΓêÆ + + ΓêÆ`. Plate offset cancels across a1 pairs,
38	amplifier offset across a0 pairs, and the a2 (chopper) reversal removes
39	second-order residuals. Global sign is fixed empirically with a known
40	magnet ΓÇö never from the netlist.
41	
42	| state | a2 a1 a0 | demod sign |
43	|---|---|---|
44	| 0 | 0 0 0 | + |
45	| 1 | 0 0 1 | ΓêÆ |
46	| 2 | 0 1 0 | + (a1 flip: plate-offset pair with 0) |
47	| 3 | 0 1 1 | ΓêÆ |
48	| 4 | 1 0 0 | ΓêÆ (a2 flip: chopper reversal) |
49	| 5 | 1 0 1 | + |
50	| 6 | 1 1 0 | ΓêÆ |
51	| 7 | 1 1 1 | + |
52

54	per phase and discards runt segments (see `analysis/`).

31	|---|---|---|---|---|---|
32	| 0 | 0 0 | p1 ΓåÆ p3 | p2 | p4 | +s + o |

43	**Demodulation rule (falls out of the table):**
44	`sign = +1 if (a0 == a2) else ΓêÆ1` ΓÇö a1 does not enter the sign.
45	Multiply the output by `sign`, blank the start of each phase, average over 8 states ΓåÆ
46	- Hall term s survives with full weight,
47	- sensor offset o cancels (spinning),
48	- amplifier offset/drift e cancels (chopping via sense-swap + current reversal).

60	## 2. Discrepancies & gotchas found (fix/verify before first power)
61	
62	1. **EN is not tied high on the PCB.** In sim EN = +5 V permanently; on the board EN comes from J3.4 with a pulldown. **All switches are OFF by default.** Drive EN high (ΓëÑ2 V) or nothing works. This is safe-by-default but a classic "board looks dead" trap.
63	2. **J3 has no ground pin.** The logic source (Pico/counter/function-gen) return must be bonded to board analog ground GND1 separately ΓÇö use the J4 SMA shell, a capacitor ground pad, or solder a dedicated ground wire. Without it, logic levels float and mux switching will be erratic.
64	3. **Component values are not in the KiCad schematic/netlist** (all read generic "R"/"C"). The as-built values exist only in your BOM/assembly. Before power, audit with a DMM against the sim: R1 Γëê 60.4 ╬⌐ (in-circuit reads Γëê 59.8 ╬⌐ because the AD8429's internal 6 k╬⌐ is in parallel), R2 = R3 = 2.2 k, R4 = 10 k, R5ΓÇôR8 pulldowns (10 k-ish), and **record R9/R10** ΓÇö you'll use them as current-sense resistors. Then back-annotate values into KiCad so the files are the single source of truth.
65	4. **External current source required.** Options in order of preference: (a) SMU (Keithley 24xx) at 100 ┬╡A, compliance ┬▒2 V; (b) REF200 (two 100 ┬╡A sources in one DIP/SOIC, ┬▒0.5 %, 25 ppm/┬░C) powered from a 9 V battery ΓÇö beautifully floating and quiet; (c) bench supply + large series resistor (crude; tempco of R dominates). The source **must float** (both terminals swing and get polarity-reversed by the a2 chopper ΓÇö the chopper reverses the *connection*, so even a unipolar source works). Compliance needed is small: plate Γëê 650 ╬⌐ + two mux channels Γëê few hundred ╬⌐ ΓåÆ < 0.2 V at 100 ┬╡A.
66	5. **RS6-2415D is a switching converter** (isolated, 9ΓÇô36 V in, ┬▒15 V out). Expect ripple/spurs in the 100s-of-kHz range on the rails. AD8429 PSRR is high but falls with frequency; spurs can alias into your sampled demod band. Verify the output spectrum in Week 1; mitigations if needed: ferrite + electrolytic bodge on the rails, battery input, or accept (demod rejects out-of-band well). Note there is **no header to inject clean bench ┬▒15 V** ΓÇö the DC/DC is the only rail path, so characterize it early.
67	6. **The 2.2 k bias-return resistors load the plate.** Differential source impedance Γëê plate (~650 ╬⌐) + 2├ù ADG1209 Ron (~120 ╬⌐ each) Γëê 0.9 k╬⌐ against a 4.4 k╬⌐ differential load ΓåÆ the amp sees only Γëê 83 % of the open-circuit Hall voltage. This is *identical in sim and hardware* and is absorbed by end-to-end calibration ΓÇö but remember it when comparing your bench slope to wafer-level S_I Γëê 60 V/A/T. Per-channel Ron mismatch also converts a small fraction of offset into residual after demod; you'll measure that in the sensorless test.
68	7. **Output drives coax directly** (AD8429 ΓåÆ J4 SMA, 10 k shunt). Watch for ringing with long cables/high C-load; keep the bench cable short, and if you see peaking, add an inline attenuator or a short series-R adapter at the SMA.
69	8. **Bandwidth trade vs. the 2023 deployment.** The published voltage-bias chain had 1 MHz bandwidth; the spun chain is ~1ΓÇô2 kHz. Fine for coil ramp (800 ms) and stored-energy tracking (ms), not for fast MHD. Options if you want both in August: record the *raw* v_meas continuously and demodulate offline (keeps everything), and/or use the static-phase "fast mode" ΓÇö now implemented as the mode-2 firmware (`pico2_static_bias_p2p4.py`, ┬º6.3), which freezes a0/a1/a2 on the p2/p4 axis; for fast events record v_meas on the scope rather than the Pico ADC.
70	9. **DSUB harness pairing:** make the cable with twisted pairs DSUB(1,2) = sensor p1&p3 (bias pair) and DSUB(6,7) = p2&p4 (sense pair). That pairing minimizes pickup loop area; pins 3,4,5,8,9 are spare (consider grounding one to GND1 as a shield/drain later).

124	### Demod reference implementation
125	Only 2 scope channels are used ΓÇö v_meas (J4) and sync (Pico GP19). a0/a1/a2 are never wired to the scope; the phase index at each sample is reconstructed from the sync pulse (high only during state 0) plus the known phase rate f. This is implemented in `hsx_demod_scope_csv.py` (run it directly on your CSV export); the core logic:
126	```python
127	import numpy as np
128	
129	def reconstruct_phase(t, sync, f, thresh=1.65):
130	    above = sync > thresh
131	    rising = np.flatnonzero(np.diff(above.astype(int)) == 1) + 1
132	    t0 = t[rising[0]]                                   # first state-0 edge
133	    phase = np.floor((t - t0) * f).astype(np.int64) % 8
134	    phase[t < t0] = -1                                   # unknown before first edge
135	    return phase
136	
137	def demodulate(t, v, sync, f, blank_frac=0.3):
138	    phase = reconstruct_phase(t, sync, f)
139	    valid = phase >= 0
140	    v, phase = v[valid], phase[valid]
141	    sign = np.where((phase & 1) == ((phase >> 2) & 1), 1.0, -1.0)   # a0==a2 rule
142	    edges = np.flatnonzero(np.diff(phase)) + 1                      # phase boundaries
143	    segs = np.split(np.arange(len(v)), edges)
144	    vals, sgns = [], []
145	    for idx in segs:
146	        if len(idx) < 10:                                           # runt segment
147	            continue
148	        keep = idx[int(blank_frac * len(idx)):]                     # blanking
149	        vals.append(v[keep].mean()); sgns.append(sign[keep[0]])
150	    vals, sgns = np.array(vals), np.array(sgns)
151	    demod = np.convolve(vals * sgns, np.ones(8) / 8, mode='valid')   # rolling 8-phase average
152	    return vals, sgns, demod
153	```

233	## 7. Low-budget calibration testbench (target < $100 in parts)
234	
235	### 7.1 Helmholtz pair (the field source *and* your primary standard)
236	A Helmholtz coil is a *calculable* standard: B = (4/5)^{3/2}┬╖┬╡0┬╖N┬╖I / R = 0.7155┬╖┬╡0┬╖N┬╖I/R, uniform to <0.1 % within ┬▒0.1 R of center (your 200 ┬╡m die + LCC alignment is trivially inside this).
237	
238	**Recipe:** mean radius R = 50 mm, spacing = R, N = 100 turns/coil of AWG 20ΓÇô22 magnet wire, series-connected (fields aiding), on a 3D-printed former with a printed cradle that registers the LCC/DSUB fixture at center, sensor plane ΓèÑ axis.
239	- k = B/I Γëê **1.8 mT/A** ΓåÆ ┬▒1.5 A gives ┬▒2.7 mT (plenty to fit a slope; output Γëê ┬▒1.6 mV ΓÇö well above the ~15 ┬╡V noise floor after demod averaging).
240	- Winding resistance Γëê 3.3 ╬⌐ (AWG 22) ΓåÆ ~5 V, ~7 W at 1.5 A: fine for sweeps, duty-cycle for long runs (or use AWG 20).
241	- Drive: bench supply in current mode for DC points; scope wavegen (possibly through a small audio amp) for AC and shot-replay.
242	
243	### 7.2 Traceability ΓÇö triangulate the coil constant three ways
244	1. **Geometry** (primary): measure mean winding radius and spacing with calipers ΓåÆ k from the formula. Dominant uncertainty is the finite winding-bundle cross-section; ~1ΓÇô2 % achievable. Measure current with a 4-wire 0.1 % shunt (e.g., 1 ╬⌐) + DMM.
245	2. **AC pickup coil** (independent physics): wind N_p Γëê 50 turns on a printed 10 mm form of known area; drive the Helmholtz at 1 kHz; V_rms = 2╧Ç f N_p A B_rms ΓåÆ k to ~2ΓÇô3 %.
246	3. **Commercial sensor cross-check** (your original idea ΓÇö good, use it as the *check*, not the primary): DRV5055A1 breakout (analog, 100 mV/mT, ┬▒21 mT) and/or TLE493D-W2B6 or MLX90393 (digital I┬▓C via the Pico, sub-┬╡T resolution). These are ┬▒2ΓÇô5 % class parts; agreement of all three methods within a few % validates the bench.
247	4. **High-field extension (free/borrowed):** the Helmholtz can't reach HSX's ~0.5 T. Two paths: (a) borrow electromagnet + gaussmeter time (the lab's prior high-T Hall characterization implies access); (b) **use HSX coil-only shots as the in-situ high-field reference** ΓÇö the vacuum field at your sensor location is computable from coil currents via the HSX field model, and this directly delivers the "in-situ cross-reference with established HSX diagnostics" flagged as future work in the Letters paper. Ask the UW team for the modeled |B| at your mounting location vs. coil current.
248	
249	### 7.3 "Accuracy of calibration" protocol
250	1. **Calibrate:** bipolar sweep, fit V_demod = m┬╖B + b on a training subset of field points.
251	2. **Verify:** apply held-out field values (interleaved, both polarities, plus a few AC amplitudes and one elevated temperature); predict B from m and compare to the coil-constant reference ΓåÆ report % error vs field, worst-case and RMS.
252	3. **Close the loop on first principles:** compare m to G┬╖S_I┬╖I┬╖(loading) ΓÇö should agree within the loading-factor uncertainty; a large gap means a wiring/value surprise.
253	4. **Uncertainty budget** (expected): coil constant 1.5ΓÇô2 %, current 0.1 %, alignment cos-error (<3┬░) 0.15 %, temperature 0.1ΓÇô0.5 %, noise Γë¬ 0.1 % after averaging ΓåÆ **~2 % absolute, <0.5 % relative/linearity** ΓÇö a major step from "uncalibrated," and honest to quote in the next paper.

1	# Second test setup ΓÇö static DC bias (p2 ΓåÆ p4), sense p1/p3
2	
3	**Prepared:** July 8, 2026 ┬╖ **Firmware:** `firmware/pico2/pico2_static_bias_p2p4.py` (mode 2)
4	**Companion (first) setup:** full current-spinning + oscilloscope DAQ ΓÇö `firmware/pico2/pico2_spin_scope.py` (mode 1), plan ┬º4.
5	
6	This document defines the project's second bench setup: the **classic
7	direct DC Hall measurement**, run through the existing readout board.
8	The external current source biases plate ports **p2 and p4**; the
9	voltage difference between ports **p1 and p3** is measured through the
10	AD8429 (G = 100.3) and digitized by the **Pico 2's own ADC** at J4 ΓÇö no
11	oscilloscope, no spinning. It complements, and never replaces, the spun
12	setup: it trades offset cancellation for simplicity, portability, and
13	full amplifier bandwidth.
14	
15	## 1. What it is for
16	
17	| Use | Why this setup |
18	|---|---|
19	| Sensor health check (bench or at HSX) | one Pico + one battery current source; 30-second answer, no scope cart |
20	| **Raw plate-offset measurement at 100 ┬╡A** | at zero applied field the chopped result *is* the plate offset ΓÇö the gen-2 die incoming-inspection number (project 03, plan ┬º2.1) |
21	| Continuity with the 2023 measurement style | the Letters deployment was static-biased; this reproduces that mode on the new hardware for apples-to-apples checks |
22	| "Fast mode" fallback | static phases = no demod bandwidth limit (~1ΓÇô2 kHz in the spun setup); the chain runs at full amplifier bandwidth, and the recording instrument becomes the bottleneck |
23	
24	## 2. Configuration
25	
26	The board's muxes are parked in the four spinning states whose bias axis
27	is p2/p4 and whose sense pair is p1/p3 ΓÇö the a1 = 1 subset of the
28	verified phase table (`docs/SPECS.md`):
29	
30	| state | a2 a1 a0 | bias | in+ | inΓêÆ | amp input (ideal) | chop sign |
31	|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
32	| 2 | 0 1 0 | p2 ΓåÆ p4 | p3 | p1 | +(s ΓêÆ o) + e | + |
33	| 3 | 0 1 1 | p2 ΓåÆ p4 | p1 | p3 | ΓêÆ(s ΓêÆ o) + e | ΓêÆ |
34	| 6 | 1 1 0 | p4 ΓåÆ p2 | p3 | p1 | ΓêÆ(s ΓêÆ o) + e | ΓêÆ |
35	| 7 | 1 1 1 | p4 ΓåÆ p2 | p1 | p3 | +(s ΓêÆ o) + e | + |
36	
37	s = Hall term, o = plate resistive offset (p2/p4 bias axis), e =
38	amplifier input offset; v_meas = G ├ù loading ├ù (amp input), with
39	G = 100.3 and loading Γëê 0.83 (SPECS). The primary state is **2**; the
40	firmware's `measure_chopped()` steps through all four.
41	
42	**What cancels, what doesn't.** Averaging the four states with signs
43	{+, ΓêÆ, ΓêÆ, +} (the a0 == a2 rule) cancels the **amplifier offset e
44	exactly** ΓÇö sense swap plus current reversal, the same chopper physics
45	as the spun system ΓÇö and the plain mean of the four states measures e
46	itself. The **plate offset o does not cancel**: with a single bias axis,
47	s and o are inseparable in principle; the chopped result is
48	x = (s ΓêÆ o) ┬╖ loading ┬╖ G. Rotating the bias axis 90┬░ (the a1 flip, i.e.
49	the full 8-state spin of the first setup) is precisely what separates
50	them. At zero applied field, x reduces to the raw plate offset ΓÇö which
51	is exactly the number incoming inspection wants.
52	
53	## 3. Wiring
54	
55	Identical to the spun setup on J3, plus the ADC tap; the scope is not
56	connected (sync GP19 is driven low).
57	
58	| Connection | Detail |
59	|---|---|
60	| Pico GP16/17/18 ΓåÆ J3 pins 3/2/1 | a0/a1/a2 (same as mode 1) |
61	| Pico GP20 ΓåÆ J3 pin 4 | EN ΓÇö board is dead until ΓëÑ 2 V (on-board pulldown) |
62	| Pico GND (pin 23) ΓåÆ GND1 | **mandatory** ΓÇö J3 has no ground pin |
63	| Pico GP26/ADC0 (pin 31) ΓåÉ J4 SMA center | v_meas tap; the on-board 10 k shunt (R4) stays |
64	| Pico AGND (pin 33) ΓåÆ J4 shell / GND1 | short ADC return |
65	| External 100 ┬╡A source ΓåÆ J2 (ΓêÑ J7) | must float; the a2 chopper reverses the *connection*, so a unipolar source works |
66	| Current verification | R9 = R10 = 100 ╬⌐ sense drops: 10.0 mV each at 100 ┬╡A, TP6ΓåÆTP5 and TP8ΓåÆTP7, **floating DMM only** (a grounded probe shorts the loop) |
67	
68	**ADC limits ΓÇö read before trusting numbers.**
69	- The RP2350 ADC is unipolar 0ΓÇô3.3 V; the AD8429 output is bipolar. Any
70	  state that drives v_meas negative clamps to ~0 V (the firmware warns).
71	  Since the chop sequence flips the signal's sign between states, a
72	  large-offset sensor will clamp in roughly half the states.
73	- 12-bit on 3.3 V = 0.8 mV/LSB; ~few-hundred ┬╡V effective after the
74	  firmware's 256├ù oversampling. Resolves the ┬▒26 mV emulator step at the
75	  percent level; does **not** resolve Earth's field (~30 ┬╡V at v_meas)
76	  or Helmholtz-scale signals (┬▒1.5ΓÇô1.8 mV). Calibration-grade numbers
77	  always come from the spun setup + scope.
78	- Optional level-shift network for bipolar readings: 100 k╬⌐ from Pico
79	  3V3 to the ADC node, 100 k╬⌐ from the node to J4 center, 100 nF from
80	  the node to AGND (the RC is fine for DC work). This centers 0 V at
81	  ~1.65 V with a ├ù0.5 scale ΓÇö then set `ADC_OFFSET_V Γëê 1.65` (measure
82	  it: short J4 to GND1 and read) and `ADC_SCALE = 0.5` in the firmware.
83	- No network and a negative-reading state? Use the states that read
84	  positive and infer the rest by symmetry, or take that state on a
85	  floating DMM at J4 (the firmware's mux parking works for DMM
86	  measurements too).
87	
88	## 4. Procedure
89	
90	1. Cold checks done (plan ┬º4 Day 1); board powered, ┬▒15 V verified;
91	   Pico GND bonded to GND1.
92	2. External source connected at J2, verified via the R9/R10 drops
93	   (10.0 mV each at 100 ┬╡A); cross-check V(R9)/R9 = V(R10)/R10 ΓÇö a
94	   mismatch means leakage.
95	3. Boot the Pico ΓåÆ mode `2` ΓåÆ `on` (EN high, state 010).
96	   Confirm EN at TP4, a1 high at TP2, a0/a2 low at TP3/TP1.
97	4. Connect the emulator plug (first time) or sensor. **Always `off`
98	   before touching the DSUB.**
99	5. `read` ΓÇö single-state sanity number. `chop` ΓÇö the amplifier-offset-
100	   free measurement; record x and e. `log 600 2` ΓÇö ten-minute drift log
101	   as CSV over USB serial (capture on the host, plot).
102	6. Done: `off`, then disconnect.
103	
104	## 5. Expected numbers
105	
106	| Condition | Expectation |
107	|---|---|
108	| Emulator plug, zero field | per-state ┬▒Γëê 26 mV around e; chopped \|x\| Γëê **26 mV** (same magnitude as the p1/p3-axis states, opposite sign ΓÇö the emulator's ╬öR arm produces equal-magnitude o on both axes) |
109	| Real sensor, zero field | x = raw plate offset ├ù 0.83 ├ù 100.3 ΓÇö **record it; that is the measurement.** Repeat 180┬░-flipped and average pairs to reject ambient field |
110	| Sensor + NdFeB magnet waved close | tens of mV swing, clearly visible in `log` output ΓÇö the quick sanity/sign check |
111	| Sensor + Earth's field | ~30 ┬╡V at v_meas ΓÇö below this setup's ADC resolution; don't chase it here |
112	| Amplifier offset e | Γë▓ few mV at v_meas (AD8429 V_os Γëñ 50 ┬╡V typ ├ù G Γëê 5 mV worst-case-ish); should be stable session-to-session |
113	
114	Sign convention: as everywhere in this project, the global sign is fixed
115	empirically with a magnet of known polarity ΓÇö never from the netlist.
116	
117	## 6. Relationship to the two projects
118	
119	- **Project 02 (this project):** steps 3ΓÇô5 slot into the bring-up plan
120	  as the scope-free variant of the Day-3 static-state survey, and the
121	  drift log complements the Week-3 overnight run. See plan ┬º6.3.
122	- **Project 03 (vector probe / RSI):** this is the standard tool for the
123	  gen-2 die **raw-offset distribution at 100 ┬╡A** (RSI plan ┬º2.1) ΓÇö one
124	  packaged die at a time in the LCC breakout, `chop` per die, log the
125	  distribution, pick matched dies for the cube.

1	# RSI 2026ΓÇô27: Calibrated vector Hall probe in HSX ΓÇö experiment & publication plan
2	
3	**Working title:** *A calibrated three-axis AlGaN/GaN Hall-effect probe
4	with spinning-current readout for in-vessel magnetic field measurements
5	in the HSX stellarator*
6	
7	**Target journal:** Review of Scientific Instruments (regular article).
8	**Target submission:** ~March 2027. **First author:** Y. Zhao.
9	**Revised:** July 8, 2026 ΓÇö incoming-inspection tooling settled: the
10	project-02 firmware now has a dedicated static-bias mode
11	(`../02_HSX_Hall_Sensor_Readout/firmware/pico2/pico2_static_bias_p2p4.py`,
12	setup doc `../02_.../docs/second_test_setup_static_bias.md`) that
13	measures the raw plate offset at 100 ┬╡A scope-free ΓÇö the ┬º2.1 batch
14	survey tool. Reader-friendly HTML versions of the plan docs now sit next
15	to their markdown.
16	
17	**Scope statement (fixed):** this campaign measures plasma and magnetic
18	fields inside HSX. No neutron or gamma irradiation experiments are
19	performed or claimed. Radiation response is covered by the co-authored
20	TCAD modeling manuscript (Van Gorp, Dawes, Zhao, Senesky, in prep.),
21	which is cited as complementary work; experimental radiation hardness
22	appears, at most, as one sentence of outlook.
23	
24	---
25	
26	## 1. Where the trajectory stands, and the gap this paper fills
27	
28	The 2023 Sensors Letters paper established feasibility: a packaged
29	AlGaN/GaN Hall sensor survived 68 consecutive HSX shots in-vessel and
30	tracked plasma-dependent field dynamics in real time. Its own text
31	concedes the limits ΓÇö the sensor was voltage-biased with an uncalibrated
32	offset V_off, produced a single axis, and validated only by *temporal
33	correlation* with the diamagnetic loop. Its stated future work was
34	absolute calibration against HSX magnetic diagnostics, extended-duration
35	offset stability, and lower-noise readout.
36	
37	Project 02 (bench now, HSX install Aug 2026) already answers the
38	single-axis half of that list: 100 ┬╡A current bias, four-phase
39	spinning-current with polarity chopping (kills plate and amplifier
40	offsets by construction), AD8429 readout, and a traceable Helmholtz +
41	in-situ calibration path. What it does not do is measure a vector, and a
42	single scalar component is a weak instrument in a machine whose whole
43	identity is field *geometry* ΓÇö HSX is the first quasi-helically
44	symmetric stellarator, and its diagnostics literature (PfirschΓÇôSchl├╝ter
45	current measurements, equilibrium-reconstruction optimization) is about
46	field direction and structure, not just magnitude.
47	
48	The lab lineage also points at RSI specifically: the group's
49	high-temperature 2DEG sensitivity paper (Alpert et al. 2020) is an RSI
50	article, and the canonical fusion-magnetics instrument papers (e.g.
51	Strait's DIII-D magnetic diagnostic system) live there too. An
52	instrument paper ΓÇö *what was built, how it was calibrated, traceability,
53	quantified in-machine performance* ΓÇö is exactly RSI's format.
54	
55	**Thesis of the paper:** the first absolutely calibrated, multi-axis
56	(2ΓÇô3 component) GaN Hall-effect probe operated inside a stellarator,
57	with offset suppression by spinning-current demonstrated in-vessel, and
58	vector output validated quantitatively against the computed vacuum field
59	and HSX's standard diagnostics ΓÇö upgrading 2023's "temporal correlation"
60	to numbers with uncertainties.
61	
62	Contribution list (for the intro, and for reviewers):
63	1. Vector measurement: 2ΓÇô3 orthogonal AlGaN/GaN plates in one compact
64	   UHV-compatible ceramic cube package.
65	2. In-vessel spinning-current operation: offset-free readout at the
66	   probe, with measured long-sequence offset stability vs the 2023
67	   uncalibrated baseline.
68	3. Absolute calibration chain: bench Helmholtz (matrix calibration,
69	   traceable to geometry + 0.1 % shunt) anchored in situ by coil-only
70	   shots against the computed vacuum field at a surveyed probe pose.
71	4. Quantified plasma measurements: component-resolved ignition
72	   transients and discharge dynamics with an uncertainty budget.
73	
74	---
75	
76	## 2. Instrument
77	
78	### 2.1 Gen-2 sensor dies (larger bond pads)
79	
80	Pad enlargement doesn't move first-order sensitivity: S_I Γëê r_n┬╖G_H/(q┬╖n_s)
81	is set by the 2DEG sheet density and plate geometry, both unchanged. What
82	it plausibly improves is exactly what a cube package stresses ΓÇö wirebond
83	yield (especially on non-horizontal faces), bond placement tolerance, and
84	contact resistance (ΓåÆ lower 1/f contact noise and raw offset). What it
85	may quietly change is the terminal-to-terminal plate resistance and the
86	effective shape factor if the metal encroaches on the octagon.
87	
88	Incoming inspection per die, before any packaging (half a day for a
89	batch):
90	- Full 2-terminal resistance map across all pin pairs; compare against
91	  the 2023 signature (~650 ╬⌐ opposite-pair). **If R changed, update the
92	  emulator arm value (649 ╬⌐ today) and the bias-return loading factor
93	  (0.83 today) in `../02_.../docs/SPECS.md` ΓÇö the ┬▒26 mV emulator
94	  expectation moves with them.**
95	- 3-terminal contact-resistance estimate on a sample of pads.
96	- Raw offset distribution at 100 ┬╡A across the batch (pick matched dies
97	  for the cube). **Standard tool:** the second test setup from project
98	  02 ΓÇö static bias p2 ΓåÆ p4, sense p1/p3, Pico-ADC readout
99	  (`../02_.../firmware/pico2/pico2_static_bias_p2p4.py`; procedure and
100	  limits in `../02_.../docs/second_test_setup_static_bias.md`). One
101	  packaged die in the LCC breakout, `measure_chopped()` per die
102	  (amplifier offset cancels; at zero field the result *is* the raw
103	  plate offset), log the distribution.
104	- Spot-check S_I with the Helmholtz on one packaged sample; expect
105	  Γëê 60 V/A/T unchanged.
106	
107	### 2.2 Cube module
108	
109	Concept: the proven single-die process ΓÇö die ΓåÆ LCC (Spectrum), Al wedge
110	bonds, EPO-TEK 353ND encapsulation, 150 ┬░C vacuum bake ΓÇö repeated per
111	face on a machinable ceramic (or zirconia, matching the 2023 holder)
112	cube, LCCs on 2 or 3 mutually orthogonal faces. Nothing new is qualified
113	except the cube itself and the face-mount adhesive/bake compatibility.
114	
115	Design points to settle in September:
116	- Cube size: set by LCC footprint + routing clearance; keep the probe
117	  head compact enough for the existing standoff/graphite-shield concept
118	  (shield likely needs a resize, not a redesign).
119	- Face flatness/orthogonality spec: the calibration matrix absorbs
120	  fixed misalignment, so ┬▒1┬░ machining is acceptable ΓÇö but it must be
121	  *stable* through bake and thermal cycling.
122	- Bond accessibility on vertical faces: this is the yield risk the
123	  larger pads exist to mitigate. Plan a mechanical-sample bond trial
124	  before committing flight dies.
125	- 2 vs 3 axes: build for 3; if bond yield or feedthrough pins force it,
126	  a 2-axis module is still a publishable vector instrument (state the
127	  choice honestly in the paper).
128	
129	### 2.3 Readout: replicate the 02 board per axis
130	
131	Decision: **three copies of `hsx_2026_v1`** rather than a new
132	multi-channel board rev. Rationale: the gerber/order package already
133	exists (`../02_.../circuit/hsx_setup_v1_Y23.zip`, hand-assembly ΓÇö budget
134	real bench days for two more builds), the design will have a full
135	bring-up campaign of heritage by September, and channel isolation comes
136	free (independent amps, independent floating supplies). A rev-B

188	## 3. Calibration plan (the heart of the paper)
189	
190	### 3.1 Per-axis scalar calibration
191	Reuse the project-02 Week-3 protocol per channel: bipolar Helmholtz
192	sweeps (┬▒2.7 mT), sensitivity-vs-bias linearity at 50/100/200/500 ┬╡A,
193	AC response 10 HzΓÇô3 kHz, hotplate 25ΓÇô100 ┬░C coefficient, overnight
194	drift. Targets unchanged: ~2 % absolute, < 0.5 % linearity.
195	
196	### 3.2 Vector (matrix) calibration
197	Model: **v = M┬╖B + b**, with v the three demodulated outputs, M a 3├ù3
198	matrix (per-axis gains on the diagonal, misalignment + cross-sensitivity
199	off-diagonal), b residual offsets (should be ~0 with spinning ΓÇö measure
200	it anyway; it's a headline number).
201	
202	Method: single-axis Helmholtz + a 3D-printed indexing cradle that holds
203	the cube in each of the six ┬▒face orientations (90┬░ indexed) plus two
204	45┬░ checks. At each orientation, sweep B over ┬▒2.5 mT and record all
205	three channels. Least-squares fit of M and b (24+ sweep-orientation
206	combinations, 12 unknowns ΓÇö well over-determined; report residuals).
207	Extract and report the misalignment angles from the polar decomposition
208	of M ΓÇö expect ~1ΓÇô2┬░ from assembly. Checks: planar-Hall cross-talk (drive
209	B in-plane of each die, confirm second-order), per-die temperature
210	coefficient (cube on hotplate), repeatability after a thermal cycle and
211	after re-mounting in the cradle.
212	
213	### 3.3 In-situ absolute anchor (the RSI centerpiece)
214	HSX coil-only shots produce a vacuum field that is *computable* at any
215	point from the coil currents and geometry. With the probe pose (position
216	+ orientation) surveyed on its mount, the predicted vector **B_vac** at
217	the probe is compared against **MΓü╗┬╣(v ΓêÆ b)** ΓÇö a quantitative,
218	component-by-component absolute check inside the machine, at multiple
219	field settings. This single figure upgrades the 2023 paper's
220	correlation-only validation into calibration traceability, and it is
221	what makes the paper an instruments paper rather than a demo. Requires:
222	(a) surveyed mount pose (photogrammetry or fixture CAD + machinist
223	survey; ┬▒1 mm, ┬▒0.5ΓÇô1┬░ is enough for a ~2 % / ~2┬░ budget), (b) UW's
224	vacuum-field computation at that pose for the requested settings ΓÇö both
225	go in the July email.
226

236	| **Total (goal)** | **Γëñ 2ΓÇô3 % magnitude, Γëñ 2┬░ direction** | |

185	## 4. Final three-board readout architecture
186	
187	### 4.1 Why the earlier ambient star is rejected
188	
189	The live netlist connects R2.1 and R3.2 to local `GND1`, with `/in+` through R2 and `/in-`
190	through R3. R2=R3=2.2 kohm. If two board GND1 nodes are joined by scope BNC shells or an ambient
191	star, a selected sensor terminal in one axis can reach another axis through approximately
192	`2.2k + 2.2k + mux Ron`. That is an intentional inter-axis electrical path. An SN74LVC125A buffer
193	does not supply galvanic isolation.
194	
195	The final architecture therefore supersedes the common-GND1 decision. It is shown in
196	`drawings/50_final_isolated_readout.svg` and tabulated in `50_FINAL_AMBIENT_DOMAIN_MAP.csv`.
197	
198	### 4.2 Domain architecture
199	
200	For each axis i in X/Y/Z:
201	
202	- shared protected 24 V input -> independent fuse/current limit/disconnect -> `RS6_i` input;
203	- RS6 isolated output rails and `GND1_i` power only that board-domain circuitry;
204	- one floating, reversible 100-uA source remains wholly in the same domain;
205	- common Pico a0/a1/a2/EN enters one four-line galvanic barrier for that domain;
206	- barrier outputs use local GND1_i, fail-safe defaults, local decoupling and selected series R;
207	- board J4_i enters an isolated/differential acquisition channel;
208	- all three isolated measurement channels share one timebase only after isolation;
209	- one frame-sync channel accompanies them.
210	
211	Allowed shared resources:
212	
213	- one versioned phase sequence and frame definition;
214	- input-side Pico/timing ground;
215	- protected upstream 24-V source and its input return;
216	- common DAQ timebase after the three measurement barriers;
217	- chassis/vessel/CF flange and screen termination structure;
218	- common calibration procedure.
219	
220	Required independent resources:
221	
222	- the 12 Hall terminals and their 19C circuits;
223	- the six screened pairs;
224	- GND1_X/GND1_Y/GND1_Z;
225	- three board analog chains and RS6 output rails;
226	- three 100-uA sources/returns and compliance/fault limits;
227	- three four-line isolation receiver output sides;
228	- three isolated/differential measurement front ends;
229	- per-axis gain/offset records, faults, disconnects and cartridge travelers.
230	
231	Forbidden connections:
232	
233	- GND1_i to another GND1;
234	- any GND1 to Pico/control input ground;
235	- direct grounded oscilloscope BNC shells on multiple J4 outputs;
236	- current-source return to chassis or another source;
237	- screen to a Hall terminal, J1 signal, cartridge or GND1;
238	- USB/probe/protection-earth paths that silently bridge domains.
239	
240	The RS6 barrier is functional isolation, not a protective safety rating. Protective-earth and
241	personnel safety remain governed by the laboratory system design.
242

268	### 4.4 Cable and shielding
269	
270	Use two screened pairs per axis: A carries p1/p3 and B carries p2/p4 under the fixed J1 convention.
271	Roles change during spinning; neither pair is permanently ΓÇ£biasΓÇ¥ or ΓÇ£sense.ΓÇ¥
272	
273	Each in-vessel screen stops before the cartridge guard and terminates at the CF flange. The
274	air-side continuation screen terminates to the same chassis region and floats at the board end.
275	No screen crosses the feedthrough as a signal pin. The exact hot screen clamp/contact process is
276	`G50-03`.
277	
278	KAP301 evidence gives OD `1.5 +/-0.15 mm`, 300-deg-C/UHV catalog ratings, about 77 pF/m
279	conductor-to-conductor and about 140 pF/m conductor-to-screen. Two worst-case pair cables require
280	3.30 mm; the final concept reserves 3.80 mm. This is 0.50 mm total width allowance, not a released
281	fit. Installed length, lay, bend, capacitance, abrasion, termination and proof-load testing remain
282	`G50-03`.
283	
284	### 4.5 Phase control, acquisition and performance claim
285	
286	The isolator output side must meet the board's actual a0/a1/a2/EN VIH/VIL, R5-R8, cable-C and
287	power-sequence conditions. TI requires a safe OE bias and fast edges can ring; select series
288	resistance only after far-end threshold/no-recrossing tests.
289	
290	One recombined update requires eight phase states:
291	
292	| Phase rate | Update rate before filtering |
293	|---:|---:|
294	| 40 kHz | 5 kS/s |
295	| 80 kHz | 10 kS/s |
296	| 100 kHz | 12.5 kS/s |
297	| 160 kHz | 20 kS/s |
298	
299	Do not claim 20-kHz recombined bandwidth from the retained 40-100-kHz phase range. A 10-kS/s
300	update may be possible at 80 kHz only after final cable, isolator, mux, amplifier, filter and noise
301	tests. A 20-kS/s update needs at least 160-kHz phases before settling/filter margin and is a held
302	performance target.
303	
304	The acquisition system must prove:
305	
306	- three isolated/differential simultaneous channels plus sync;
307	- input range, noise, common-mode and fault survival;
308	- bounded channel-to-channel aperture skew from a common-edge test;
309	- at least the signed raw samples per phase;
310	- raw phase truth, blanking/settling, demodulated gain/phase, crosstalk and export integrity;
311	- no DC GND1 cross-tie with every normal cable/probe/USB path connected.
312	
313	The four-channel DSOX1204G data sheet establishes channel count/sample-rate class, not galvanic
314	channel isolation or the required aperture-skew bound. Direct multi-BNC use is therefore not the
315	final baseline.
316

322	2. prove all 12 unique paths and all-pairs/chassis isolation with boards disconnected;
323	3. inspect J1 physical pin numbers and shell behavior;
324	4. select and limit all three current sources; test compliance, reversal, noise and fault energy;
325	5. verify GND1_X/Y/Z isolation with every power/control/acquisition cable installed;
326	6. power each board domain individually with EN in its safe state;
327	7. verify isolation-barrier defaults, local logic levels, ringing, skew and settling;
328	8. inject known delta-V into X/Y/Z and close the approximately 109-times anomaly;
329	9. run the full eight-phase sequence on emulator loads and acquire X/Y/Z+sync simultaneously;
330	10. connect one qualified real cartridge at a time only after the release board signs the evidence.
331
